title: Guidelines for Neuroprognostication in Critically ill Adults with Acute Ischemic Stroke

recommendations.text: Neurocritical Care Society guideline on the reliability of individual predictors and multivariate prediction models when counseling critically ill adults with acute ischemic stroke and their surrogates, developed by narrative systematic review using GRADE and PICOTS. A total of 518 articles met eligibility criteria. Predictors were categorized as reliable, moderately reliable, or not reliable; the acceptable threshold for predictors of good outcome was set lower than for predictors of poor outcome, because an inaccurate prediction of good outcome does not lead to an irreversible decision such as withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy.

recommendations.section: Predictor Judged Moderately Reliable: Early Neurological Improvement
recommendations.text: When counseling critically ill patients with AIS or their surrogates, the guideline suggests early neurological improvement (ENI) assessed 24 h following revascularization, or 24 h following admission for patients who are not candidates for revascularization, BE considered a moderately reliable predictor of GOOD functional outcome assessed at 3 months or later. A good outcome is expected in patients with recovery to an NIHSS of 0 to 1 at 24 h (weak recommendation; low quality evidence). ENI was defined as an improvement of 8 or more points on the NIHSS, or improvement to an NIHSS of 0 or 1 at 24 h; about 61-84% of such patients return to functional independence. This is the one predictor in the document that earned an affirmative endorsement, and it points toward a good outcome, not a poor one.

When counseling critically ill patients with AIS or their surrogates, the guideline suggests successful revascularization alone not be considered a reliable predictor of good functional outcome assessed at 3 months or later (weak recommendation; low quality evidence). Across thrombectomy trials, long-term recovery to functional independence was observed in fewer than half of patients in the intervention arm despite successful revascularization rates above 70%.

When counseling critically ill adults with AIS or their surrogates, the guideline separately suggests that each of the following NOT be considered a reliable predictor of poor functional outcome assessed at 3 months or later, when used alone: age; the admission NIHSS; hemorrhagic transformation; infarct size; a history of previous stroke; admission hyperglycemia; and cerebral collateral circulation status (each a weak recommendation; very low quality evidence).

When counseling critically ill patients with AIS or their surrogates, the guideline suggests that the ASTRAL score, the DRAGON / MR-DRAGON / MT-DRAGON scores, the iScore prediction model, and the THRIVE / THRIVE-c / THRIVE-EVT scores each not be considered reliable predictors of functional outcome assessed at 3 months or later (weak recommendations; quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate across the models). Apart from early neurological improvement, no individual predictor or model was considered reliable for the prediction of mortality or functional outcome.

Good practice statement: prognostication should be multimodal, with consideration of the complete clinical condition, and never based on a single variable (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Good practice statement: the assessment of neurological prognosis should be performed in the absence of potential confounders of the neurological examination, such as sedative medications, metabolic imbalances, or systemic illness (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).
Good practice statement: preexisting functional impairment and comorbidities should be considered when formulating a prognosis (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Good practice statement: counseling of critically ill patients with AIS expected to survive the index hospital admission, and/or their surrogates, should include discussion of long-term functional outcomes; discussion should not focus on day-to-day changes and in-hospital outcomes alone (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Good practice statement: acceptable outcomes for individual patients should serve as the basis for prognostication and shared decision-making (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded). The panel notes the disability paradox: some patients with marked functional disability report satisfaction with their health and quality of life.

Good practice statement: avoid premature neuroprognostication in critically ill patients with AIS, including patients with severe ischemic stroke. While early neurological improvement following revascularization may clarify a likely good outcome at 24 h, the appropriate period of observation in an individual patient should be determined with careful consideration of the anticipated evolution of neurological illness, potential confounders of the neurological examination, and completion of appropriate diagnostic imaging (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

recommendations.section: Good Practice: Time Course of Recovery
recommendations.text: Good practice statement: critically ill patients with severe AIS, and/or their surrogates, should be counseled that incremental functional recovery may occur up to 6 months and sometimes longer following the stroke, whereas most patients with AIS of mild to moderate severity will achieve the majority of their functional recovery within 3 months (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Good practice statement: critically ill patients with AIS who require artificial enteral nutrition, and/or their surrogates, should be counseled that recovery of swallow function and removal of the feeding tube is likely, but not certain, within a period of several months among survivors (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Good practice statement: critically ill patients with AIS who require tracheostomy, and/or their surrogates, should be counseled that successful decannulation is possible within a period of several months among survivors (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).

Good practice statement: discussions of prognosis and goals of care for patients with large hemispheric infarction should occur prior to neurological deterioration where feasible, to allow patients and surrogates sufficient time to make informed decisions on decompressive craniectomy and other therapeutic interventions (strong recommendation, evidence cannot be graded).
